cards.summary: A large reddish-brown cockroach, about 3.5 to 4 cm long, that often lives in drains, sewers and damp areas and comes indoors at night. It can carry germs onto food and kitchen surfaces.
signs: Large reddish-brown cockroach with a pale yellowish band around the edge of the shield behind the head
Seen at night near drains, bathrooms, kitchens and basements; runs for cover when a light is switched on
Dark, cylindrical droppings larger than pepper grains, and dark smear marks along walls and skirting
Dark brown, purse-shaped egg cases (oothecae) about 8 mm long, dropped or glued in sheltered spots
Shed skins and a musty smell where many are present
healthRisks: Can carry bacteria and other germs from drains and waste onto food, dishes and kitchen surfaces
Droppings and shed skins contain allergens that can trigger sneezing, skin rashes and asthma
safeSteps: Keep food in sealed containers and clear crumbs, spills and dirty dishes before night
Fix leaking taps and pipes and wipe sinks and floors dry; cockroaches need water
Fit fine mesh or tight covers on floor drains, and keep drain traps filled with water
Seal cracks and gaps around pipes, drains, doors and walls
Empty garbage daily into a bin with a tight lid, and remove clutter such as cardboard and paper piles
Place small covered insect monitoring traps inside cupboards, under sinks and behind appliances, out of reach of lizards, pets and children, and check them daily
callProfessionalWhen: Cockroaches are seen in daylight or in large numbers
Numbers do not drop after two to three weeks of cleaning and sealing
They come from building drains or sewers you cannot reach, or the problem is in a food business, hostel or hospital

cards.summary: A small light-brown cockroach, about 1.3 to 1.6 cm long, with two dark stripes behind the head. It lives indoors, mainly in kitchens and bathrooms, and can build up large numbers quickly.
signs: Small tan to light-brown cockroach with two dark parallel stripes on the shield behind the head
Females carrying a light-brown egg case sticking out from the tip of the body
Pepper-like specks of droppings and small dark smears in cabinets, hinges and around stoves, fridges and sinks
Many small wingless young (nymphs) of different sizes hiding in cracks
Sightings in daylight, which often mean a large population
healthRisks: Can spread germs linked to stomach upsets, diarrhoea and dysentery by walking over food and utensils
Droppings and shed skins contain allergens that can trigger skin rashes, sneezing and asthma
safeSteps: Wipe up spills and crumbs, wash dishes before night, and do not leave pet food out overnight
Store flour, sugar, cereals and other foods in airtight containers
Empty garbage every night into a sturdy bin with a lid
Fix leaks and seal holes where pipes pass through walls, and cracks in kitchens and bathrooms
Check grocery bags, cartons and second-hand appliances before bringing them inside
Place ten or more small covered insect monitoring traps inside cupboards, under sinks and behind appliances for a week, out of reach of lizards, pets and children, and check them daily
callProfessionalWhen: Cockroaches are seen in daylight
They are spread across several rooms or flats in a building
The problem is in a kitchen that serves the public, a hostel or a hospital

names.en: Other cockroach (oriental, brown-banded, Australian and others)

cards.summary: Several other cockroach species live in and around homes, including the dark oriental cockroach of damp drains and basements, the small brown-banded cockroach of warm dry rooms, and the Australian cockroach. They are managed in much the same way.
signs: Very dark brown to nearly black, about 2.5 cm, slow-moving cockroach near drains, damp floors and basements (oriental cockroach)
Small cockroach with two light bands across the wings or body, found high up in furniture, cupboards and electronics (brown-banded cockroach)
Reddish-brown cockroach like the American cockroach but with pale yellow streaks at the base of the wings (Australian cockroach)
Droppings, egg cases and shed skins in sheltered, undisturbed places
healthRisks: Can carry germs from drains and waste onto food and surfaces
Droppings and shed skins contain allergens that can trigger asthma and other allergies
safeSteps: Keep food sealed and clear crumbs, spills and dirty dishes before night
Fix leaks, dry damp areas and improve ventilation in basements and bathrooms
Cover floor drains with fine mesh and seal cracks around pipes and walls
Reduce clutter such as stacked paper, cardboard and unused furniture
Place small covered insect monitoring traps inside cupboards, under sinks and behind appliances, out of reach of lizards, pets and children, and check them daily
callProfessionalWhen: Cockroaches are seen in daylight or in large numbers
Numbers do not drop after two to three weeks of cleaning and sealing

cards.summary: A common grey fly, about 6 to 7 mm long, that breeds in garbage, manure and rotting organic matter. It can carry germs from waste onto food.
signs: Grey fly with four dark lengthwise stripes on the back behind the head
Flies landing on food, garbage and waste, often in large numbers in warm weather
Small dark specks (fly spots) on walls, windows and light fittings
Small white maggots in garbage, compost, manure or animal bedding
Steady buzzing near windows and lights
healthRisks: Can carry germs from waste and faeces onto food, linked to diarrhoea, dysentery, cholera, other food-borne illness and eye infections
Large numbers near animal sheds or garbage dumps are a hygiene concern
safeSteps: Keep food and drinking water covered, and wash fruit and vegetables before eating
Put garbage in bags inside bins with tight lids, and empty and wash bins at least weekly
Remove animal manure, pet waste and rotting food often; this is where maggots develop
Fit window and door screens and keep them in good repair
Use fly swatters, or light traps placed away from where food is prepared
Turn compost so it heats up, or keep it covered and away from the house
callProfessionalWhen: Flies keep appearing indoors after garbage and waste have been removed
Large numbers come from nearby animal sheds, drains or a dump; report this to your local municipal health office

cards.summary: A small black mosquito with white stripes on its legs and body that bites mainly in the daytime. It breeds in clean water held in containers around homes and can spread dengue, chikungunya and Zika.
signs: Small (about 3 to 5 mm) black mosquito with white bands on the legs and white markings on the body
Bites during the day, especially in the early morning and late afternoon, often on ankles and legs
Rests indoors in dark corners, under furniture and on hanging clothes, curtains or umbrellas
Wriggling larvae in water in coolers, drums, buckets, tanks, flower vases, plant saucers, old tyres, coconut shells or fridge drip trays
High-pitched whine close to the ear
healthRisks: Can spread dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses

Dengue can become severe, usually after the fever goes down; warning signs include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, fast breathing, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, and extreme tiredness or restlessness
A second dengue infection carries a higher risk of severe dengue
Chikungunya causes fever with severe joint pain that can last for months
Zika infection in pregnancy can cause birth defects such as an abnormally small head; pregnant women with fever, rash or red eyes should see a doctor
safeSteps: Get medical care and a test at a health centre promptly if anyone has a fever, and go to hospital at once for any dengue warning sign
Once a week, empty, scrub and dry coolers, buckets, drums, flower vases and plant saucers before refilling them
Cover water tanks and storage containers tightly, and throw away tyres, tins, bottles and coconut shells that can hold rainwater
Clear roof gutters and fridge drip trays so water does not stand
Wear clothes that cover arms and legs, use window screens, and use a mosquito net for daytime sleep, especially for babies, the sick and the elderly
callProfessionalWhen: Larvae are breeding where you cannot empty the water, such as overhead tanks, construction sites or blocked drains; inform your local health department, municipal vector-control team or ASHA worker
Several people nearby have fever at the same time
firstAid: Get medical care for any fever after mosquito bites; do not wait for it to get worse
Go to a hospital immediately for any dengue warning sign
Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen for a fever that could be dengue, as they can increase bleeding; ask a doctor or health worker what to take for the fever
Do not use papaya-leaf juice or other herbal drinks in place of medical care
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: The mosquito that spreads malaria. It bites mainly from dusk through the night and breeds in clean or slow-moving water such as rain pools, rice fields, wells, tanks and irrigation channels.
signs: Mosquito that often rests with its body at an angle to the wall, head down and tail up (some Indian species sit flatter)
Pale and dark spots or patches on the wings in many species
Bites starting soon after dusk and continuing through the night
Larvae lying flat just under the water surface instead of hanging down
Breeding in rain pools, puddles, rice fields, wells, irrigation channels, water tanks and construction sites
healthRisks: Spreads malaria, which usually starts with fever, chills and headache 10 to 15 days after an infective bite
Malaria can become severe quickly, especially in young children, pregnant women and travellers
In parts of Africa and some other regions Anopheles also spread lymphatic filariasis; in mainland India it is spread mainly by Culex
safeSteps: Get medical care and a malaria test at a health centre promptly for any fever, chills or headache; early testing matters
Sleep under a mosquito net, and fit window and door screens
Wear clothes that cover arms and legs in the evening and at night
Drain or fill puddles and pits around the home, and cover wells, tanks and water containers
Keep water from collecting at construction sites, in tyres and in discarded containers
callProfessionalWhen: Larvae are found in wells, tanks, ponds or fields you cannot drain; tell your local health department or ASHA worker
Several people in the area have fever
firstAid: Get medical care and a malaria test for any fever after mosquito bites
Go to a hospital immediately for confusion, fits, breathing difficulty, dark urine, yellow eyes, unusual bleeding, extreme weakness, or being unable to sit, eat or drink
Follow the health worker's advice to the end, even after feeling better; some malaria can come back weeks or months later, so get tested again if fever returns
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: A plain brownish mosquito that bites mainly at night and breeds in dirty or polluted standing water such as drains, septic tanks and ditches. In India it can spread lymphatic filariasis and Japanese encephalitis.
signs: Plain brown mosquito that rests with its body parallel to the wall
Bites at night, often with a loud whine around sleeping areas
Larvae hanging head-down from the water surface in drains, cesspits, septic tanks, ditches and stagnant water
Small raft-like clusters of eggs floating on dirty water
Large numbers near rice fields and pig sheds in rural areas
healthRisks: The common house Culex (Culex quinquefasciatus), which breeds in drains, cesspits and septic tanks in towns and villages, spreads lymphatic filariasis, which can cause long-term swelling of the legs, arms or scrotum
Rural Culex, especially around rice fields, pigs and water birds, spreads Japanese encephalitis, a serious brain infection
Can also spread West Nile virus
safeSteps: Get medical care quickly for fever with headache, vomiting, confusion, fits or a stiff neck, especially in children
Sleep under a mosquito net and fit screens on windows and doors
Keep drains flowing and covered, and fit mesh on septic tank vent pipes and soak-pit openings
Do not let wastewater stand near the house; drain or fill ditches and pits
Follow your local health worker's advice during filaria prevention campaigns, and ask about Japanese encephalitis vaccination where it is offered
callProfessionalWhen: Blocked or overflowing drains, septic tanks or sewage you cannot fix; report them to your municipal office or health department
firstAid: Get urgent medical care for fever with headache, vomiting, confusion, fits or a stiff neck
See a doctor for new swelling of a limb, repeated fever with painful swollen glands, or swelling of the scrotum
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: A small, flat, reddish-brown insect, about 5 mm long as an adult, that hides in beds and furniture and feeds on blood at night. It is not known to spread disease, but bites can itch and infestations are hard to clear.
signs: Flat, oval, wingless reddish-brown insects in mattress seams, bed frames, headboards and furniture joints
Small rusty or dark spots (droppings or blood) on sheets and mattress seams
Pale shed skins and tiny white eggs in crevices
Itchy bite marks, sometimes in a line, that may appear a day or more after sleeping
A sweet, musty smell in heavy infestations
healthRisks: Not known to spread disease, but bites can itch and scratching can lead to skin infection
Rarely, bites cause a strong allergic reaction
Infestations can cause poor sleep and anxiety
safeSteps: Check mattress seams, bed frames, headboards and nearby furniture with a torch
Wash bedding and clothes in hot water and dry them on the hottest setting the fabric allows
Vacuum mattress seams, bed frames, carpet edges and cracks, then seal the vacuum contents in a bag and put it outside
Fit a zippered mattress encasement made for bed bugs, and reduce clutter around the bed
Move the bed slightly away from the wall and place interceptor cups under the legs to monitor
Check luggage after travel, and inspect second-hand furniture before bringing it home
callProfessionalWhen: Bed bugs are found in more than one room or keep coming back
You live in a hostel, hotel or apartment block where they can spread between units
The infestation is large or has spread; call a licensed pest-control professional
firstAid: Wash bites with soap and water and avoid scratching
See a doctor if bites become infected or for any strong allergic reaction

cards.summary: Small, pale, soft-bodied insects that live in colonies in the soil and eat wood, paper and cardboard, often unseen inside walls and frames. They travel in mud tubes and can damage buildings, furniture and stored items.
signs: Pencil-width mud tubes running up walls, foundations, door frames or pipes
Swarms of winged termites near lights after rain, and piles of shed wings on window sills
Wood that sounds hollow when tapped or crumbles, with soil packed into the tunnels
Blistered or darkened paint and wood surfaces, and damaged books, cardboard or papers
Pale, ant-like workers when a mud tube is broken open
Faint clicking or rustling inside wood or walls when the colony is disturbed
healthRisks: Not known to spread disease; the main risk is damage to wood, buildings and stored goods
safeSteps: Keep wood, cardboard and firewood off the ground and away from walls
Fix plumbing leaks, roof leaks and drainage problems so walls and foundations stay dry
Remove dead tree stumps, buried wood and building debris near the house
Keep a gap between soil or mulch and the wooden parts of the building
Repair foundation cracks, and check walls, door frames and storage areas regularly for mud tubes
Have the building inspected every few years
callProfessionalWhen: You find mud tubes, hollow wood or swarmers indoors
Before building or renovating, ask your builder how to keep wood away from soil and damp, and have the site inspected by a licensed pest-control professional
Dealing with termites in a building is specialist work; call a licensed pest-control professional rather than trying it yourself

cards.summary: Termites that live entirely inside dry wood such as furniture, door frames and roof timbers, without contact with soil. They push out tiny, hard, six-sided pellets.
signs: Small piles of hard, sand-like pellets with six ridged sides under wooden furniture, frames or beams
Tiny holes (under 2 mm) in wood surfaces through which pellets are pushed out
Winged termites flying during the day, and shed wings near windows
Wood that sounds hollow, or blistered paint on wooden surfaces
healthRisks: Not known to spread disease; the main risk is damage to wooden furniture and structures
safeSteps: Sweep up pellets and check the same spot after a few days; new pellets suggest the termites are still active
Inspect second-hand wooden furniture before bringing it home
Seal and paint exposed wood surfaces, cracks and joints
Replace small wooden items that are badly damaged
Note where pellets keep appearing to help an inspector
callProfessionalWhen: Pellets keep appearing from door frames, roof timbers or other structural wood
Damage is found in several places; call a licensed pest-control professional
Get more than one inspection report before deciding what to do

cards.summary: Several kinds of small black or dark-brown ants forage in kitchens and homes for sweets, grease and water. They are mainly a nuisance, but they can contaminate food.
signs: Lines of small black or dark-brown ants (about 2 to 3 mm) following the same trail to food or water
Ants gathered on sugar, sweets, fruit, pet food or around sinks
Tiny piles of soil or debris at cracks in floors, walls or along skirting
Winged ants appearing indoors in warm, humid weather
healthRisks: Can carry dirt and germs onto food
Most small black ants rarely bite or sting; some larger black ants can bite
safeSteps: Wipe up crumbs, grease and spills, and rinse food and drink containers before storing or throwing them out
Store sugar, sweets and other foods in sealed containers; thin plastic bags may not keep ants out
Wipe ant trails with soapy water to remove the scent trail they follow
Follow the trail to where ants enter, and seal cracks around pipes, wires, doors and windows
Fix dripping taps and remove standing water
Keep plants, mulch and branches from touching outside walls
callProfessionalWhen: Ants keep coming back after cleaning and sealing, or are nesting inside walls
You see large black ants with sawdust-like debris near wood, which may mean carpenter ants

cards.summary: Reddish-brown ants of mixed sizes, such as the tropical fire ant, that nest in soil and sting painfully, often many times, when their nest or food is disturbed. Stings can cause severe allergic reactions in some people.
signs: Reddish-brown ants of mixed sizes, about 2 to 5 mm, that swarm and climb quickly onto anything touching their nest
Loose soil mounds or patches in lawns, fields and along paths, sometimes with no clear mound
Burning stings followed a day or so later by itchy white pus-filled bumps
Nests in walls, under pavements or inside electrical and utility boxes
healthRisks: Stings burn and itch and can leave pus-filled bumps that may become infected or scar
Some people have a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), which is an emergency
Young children, older adults and people who cannot move away quickly are at higher risk of many stings
safeSteps: Stay well back from ant mounds and keep children and pets away; if stung, move away quickly, brush the ants off and get medical care for any severe reaction
Get emergency care for chest pain, swelling of the face or throat, dizziness, nausea or trouble breathing after stings
Wear shoes and gloves when working in gardens or fields
Do not disturb or dig into mounds
Keep food and drinks covered outdoors
callProfessionalWhen: Mounds are near homes, play areas or places where people sit or work
Ants are nesting inside walls or electrical boxes
firstAid: Move away from the ants and brush them off
Wash the area with soap and water, and avoid scratching or breaking the pus-filled bumps
Get emergency medical care for any sign of a severe allergic reaction
If the person has a known sting allergy and a prescribed adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector, use it and go to hospital at once
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: A tiny yellow to light-brown ant, about 2 mm long, that nests in warm, hidden spots indoors such as wall voids and near hot water pipes. It is hard to control and is a hygiene concern in hospitals and food businesses.
signs: Very small yellow, honey-coloured or light orange ants moving in trails
Ants in kitchens, bathrooms and near hot water pipes, heaters or appliances
Ants coming out of electrical outlets, cabinet gaps or from behind skirting
Ants feeding on greasy food, meat and sweets
healthRisks: Can carry germs onto food and surfaces, which is a particular concern in hospitals and clinics
safeSteps: Keep food sealed, clean up grease and spills, and take out garbage daily
Fix leaks and reduce moisture
Seal cracks and gaps around pipes, wiring and cabinets
Wipe trails with soapy water and note where the ants come from
callProfessionalWhen: Ants keep appearing in many rooms; colonies have many queens, and disturbing them can make them split and spread
The problem is in a hospital, clinic, food business or apartment block

cards.summary: A wingless, silvery, carrot-shaped insect, about 1 to 2 cm long, that hides in damp, dark places and feeds on paper, glue, starch and fabric. It is a nuisance that damages books and clothes rather than a health risk.
signs: Silvery-grey, tapered insects with three long tail threads, moving in quick, fish-like darts
Insects trapped in sinks or bathtubs, unable to climb the smooth sides
Irregular holes, scraped surfaces and yellow stains on books, papers, wallpaper and clothes
Tiny silvery scales and dust-like droppings near the damage
healthRisks: Not known to spread disease; it damages paper, books and fabrics
safeSteps: Keep bathrooms, kitchens and storage areas dry; use fans or a dehumidifier in damp rooms
Fix leaking pipes and drips
Clean dust and debris regularly, and empty and clean cupboards and storage boxes from time to time
Store books, papers and dry foods in tightly closed containers, and move stacks of paper now and then
Seal gaps around pipes and skirting
To find where they are active, leave small glass jars wrapped on the outside with tape overnight; silverfish climb in and cannot climb out
callProfessionalWhen: Damage to valuable books, documents or fabrics continues after drying and cleaning

cards.summary: A fast-moving, yellowish-grey centipede with 15 pairs of very long legs that hunts insects indoors at night. It rarely bites and is not considered medically important; seeing many may point to other insects or damp conditions.
signs: Yellowish-grey body about 2.5 to 3.5 cm long with three dark stripes and very long banded legs
Very fast movement across floors and walls, usually at night
Found in bathrooms, basements, drains and other damp, dark places
healthRisks: May give a mildly painful bite if handled
Not known to spread disease
safeSteps: Avoid handling it; guide it into a jar or onto paper and release it outdoors
Reduce damp with fans or a dehumidifier, and fix leaks
Reduce the insects it feeds on, such as cockroaches and silverfish
Seal cracks in walls and floors, and screen floor drains
Clear stored cardboard boxes and clutter from damp areas
callProfessionalWhen: Many are seen regularly, which may mean another insect problem that needs an inspection
firstAid: Wash a bite with soap and water
Get medical care for severe pain, spreading swelling or signs of an allergic reaction

cards.summary: A slow-moving, rounded, many-legged animal that lives in damp soil and leaf litter and sometimes wanders indoors in large numbers after rain. It does not bite, but some kinds release a fluid that can irritate skin and eyes.
signs: Dark brown to black, rounded, segmented body with two pairs of legs on most segments
Slow, wave-like leg movement; curls into a coil when disturbed or dead
Many appearing at doorways, porches, basements or bathrooms after heavy rain
healthRisks: Some species release a defensive fluid that can irritate or stain the skin and burn the eyes
Not known to spread disease
safeSteps: Do not handle them with bare hands; sweep them into a dustpan and move them outdoors
Clear leaf litter, compost, mulch and rotting wood from around the foundation
Seal cracks and gaps under doors
Keep basements and crawl spaces dry, and avoid overwatering near the house
callProfessionalWhen: Large numbers keep entering the house for more than a few days
firstAid: Wash skin with soap and water after contact
If fluid gets into the eyes, rinse with plenty of clean water for at least 15 minutes, removing contact lenses, and get medical care

cards.summary: A reddish-brown insect, about 1.5 to 2 cm long, with pincer-like forceps at the tail end. It hides in damp, dark places outdoors and sometimes enters homes, where it is mainly a nuisance.
signs: Long, flat, reddish-brown insect with curved (male) or straighter (female) pincers at the rear
Found under pots, stones, mulch, damp cloths and in drains, mainly at night
Ragged holes in seedlings, flowers and soft fruit in gardens
healthRisks: Can pinch if trapped in clothing or sat on
Not known to spread disease

Look-alike small orange-and-black rove beetles (Paederus) release a fluid that blisters skin if crushed; brush them off without crushing, wash the skin with soap and water, and see a doctor for blisters or eye irritation
safeSteps: Sweep or vacuum up earwigs found indoors and put them outside
Seal cracks and gaps around doors and windows
Remove leaf litter, boards and debris from near the walls, and keep gutters clear
Direct rainwater away from the house and ventilate damp spaces
Use yellow outdoor bulbs, which attract fewer insects
In gardens, set rolled newspaper or cardboard traps at dusk and empty them well away from the garden each morning
callProfessionalWhen: Large numbers keep entering the house despite these steps

cards.summary: Small, pale buff moths whose larvae feed on wool, silk, fur, feathers and other animal fibres in stored clothes and carpets. The damage is done by the larvae, not the adults.
signs: Small (about 6 mm) golden-buff moths fluttering weakly in dark wardrobes rather than flying to lights
Irregular holes in woollen, silk or fur items, often in hidden areas such as under collars
Silk tubes, webbing or small cigar-shaped cases on fabric, with droppings
Loose fur and bare patches on fur items
healthRisks: Not known to spread disease; it damages clothing, carpets and stored textiles
safeSteps: Wash woollens and other washable items in hot water, or have delicate items dry-cleaned
Freeze small items in sealed bags for several days if the fabric allows
Vacuum wardrobes, corners, under furniture and along skirting, and empty the vacuum outside promptly
Store only clean clothes, in airtight containers or sealed bags
Air and brush stored woollens in sunlight from time to time, paying attention to seams and folds
Use covered pheromone monitoring traps, hung out of reach of children, pets and lizards, to check for moths
callProfessionalWhen: Damage continues in carpets, upholstery or large collections after cleaning
Valuable textiles, heirlooms or museum items are affected

cards.summary: A small moth whose larvae feed on stored foods such as flour, rice, cereals, dried fruit, nuts and spices. The larvae leave silk webbing in food packets.
signs: Small moths, about 8 to 10 mm, with forewings pale near the body and reddish-brown with a coppery shine on the outer part
Silk webbing, clumped food and droppings inside food packets or containers
Small whitish caterpillars crawling on shelves, walls or ceilings
Small holes in food packets
healthRisks: Not known to spread disease; it spoils stored food
safeSteps: Inspect stored foods, especially opened or older packets, and throw out anything with webbing or larvae in a sealed bag outside the house
Empty and clean shelves, vacuum cracks and corners, then wash them with soap and water
Store dry foods in containers with tight-fitting lids; thin plastic bags are not enough
Freeze small amounts of flour, grains or spices for a few days before storing them
Keep only as much food as you will use soon, do not mix old and new food, and wash containers before refilling
Use covered pheromone monitoring traps placed out of reach of children, pets and lizards, and check them weekly
callProfessionalWhen: Moths keep appearing after cleaning, or the problem is in a shop, warehouse or food business

cards.summary: Small dark beetles with a long snout whose larvae develop inside whole grains such as rice, wheat and maize. Related grain weevils, including the maize and granary weevils, look and behave much the same.
signs: Small (about 2 to 4 mm) reddish-brown to black beetles with a long snout, crawling on grain, sacks or container walls
Four faint reddish or yellowish spots on the wing covers (rice and maize weevils)
Grains with round exit holes, hollow kernels and fine powdery dust in the store
Grain that feels warm or damp, or smells musty, in heavily infested stores
Very faint ticking or chewing sounds from larvae feeding inside grains, which the ear usually cannot hear
healthRisks: Not known to spread disease; it spoils stored grain and reduces its weight and quality
safeSteps: Inspect stored grain regularly and keep any infested batch apart from other grain
Clean bins, sacks and storerooms thoroughly before filling them with new grain, removing old grain and dust
Do not mix old and new grain
Store grain dry, in clean, tightly sealed containers in a cool place
Freeze small household quantities for a few days before storing them
Throw out heavily infested small packets in a sealed bag outside the house
callProfessionalWhen: The infestation is in large stores, godowns or farm bins; consult your local agricultural extension office or a licensed pest-control professional
Weevils keep reappearing after cleaning

cards.summary: Tiny, dark reddish-brown, wingless insects, up to about 3 mm, that jump and feed on the blood of pets, rats and people. Rat fleas can spread plague and murine typhus in some regions.
signs: Tiny dark insects, flattened from side to side, that jump; seen on pets, bedding or carpets
Itchy bites, often on the ankles and lower legs, each with a small red centre
Black specks of flea dirt in pet fur or bedding
Pets scratching, licking or losing hair
Fleas jumping onto white socks when walking through pet resting areas
healthRisks: Bites cause itching and can trigger allergic skin reactions in people and pets
Rat fleas can spread plague and murine typhus; plague needs urgent medical care
Fleas can pass tapeworms to pets and occasionally to children
safeSteps: Stay well back from dead rats and other dead animals and do not handle them; get medical care for fever after flea bites, and tell your local health office if you see several dead rats
Vacuum floors, carpets, furniture and pet resting areas every day or two, and empty the vacuum outside
Wash pet bedding and rugs weekly in hot soapy water
Comb pets with a fine metal flea comb, and take a pet with fleas to a veterinarian
Keep rats and stray animals out by sealing gaps and storing food in closed containers
callProfessionalWhen: Fleas remain after two to three weeks of vacuuming and washing
Fleas have come with rats in the house
firstAid: Wash bites with soap and water and avoid scratching
Get medical care quickly for fever, swollen painful glands or feeling very unwell after flea bites or contact with rats
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: Small, flat, eight-legged parasites that attach to dogs, livestock and people to feed on blood and swell after feeding. Some ticks spread serious illnesses.
signs: Flat, oval, brown or reddish animal with eight legs; swollen, grey-blue and bean-shaped after feeding
Ticks on dogs, especially on the ears, neck and between the toes, or on cattle and goats
Ticks crawling on walls, curtains and furniture near where dogs sleep (brown dog tick)
A tick attached to the skin, often in hidden places such as the scalp, behind the ears, armpits or groin
healthRisks: Some ticks spread illnesses such as Indian tick typhus (spotted fever), Kyasanur Forest Disease and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever in parts of India and Asia, and other infections worldwide
Fever, chills, aches or a rash within a few weeks of a tick bite need medical attention
Rarely, an attached tick can cause weakness or paralysis that improves after the tick is removed
safeSteps: Get medical care for fever, rash, aches or weakness after a tick bite, and mention the bite to the doctor
Wear long sleeves and trousers tucked into socks, and light-coloured clothes, in grass, bush or livestock areas
Check your body, children and pets after time outdoors or with animals
Wear gloves when removing ticks from animals or handling animal blood at slaughter
Take dogs and livestock with ticks to a veterinarian, keep grass short near the house, and vacuum cracks where dog ticks hide
callProfessionalWhen: Ticks are breeding inside the house, for example many on walls near where dogs sleep
Livestock sheds are heavily infested; contact your veterinarian or animal husbandry office
Dead monkeys are found in a Kyasanur Forest Disease area of the Western Ghats; report them to the health department
firstAid: Remove an attached tick promptly with fine-tipped tweezers: grip it close to the skin and pull out with steady, even pressure without twisting
Do not crush the tick with your fingers, and do not use heat, oil, nail polish or other substances to make it let go
After removing a tick, wash the bite and your hands with soap and water
See a doctor if fever, rash, aches or weakness develop within a few weeks, and mention the tick bite; a black scab (eschar) at a bite with fever also needs a doctor
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: Stinging insects with a narrow waist, such as paper wasps and hornets, that build paper or mud nests on buildings and trees. They can sting repeatedly when their nest is disturbed, and stings can cause dangerous allergic reactions.
signs: Slender black-and-yellow, reddish-brown or brown insects with a narrow waist and a smooth body
Umbrella-shaped, open-celled paper nests under eaves, balconies and window frames, or large enclosed paper nests in trees and roofs
Many wasps flying in and out of one hole in a wall, roof or the ground
Loud buzzing near a nest
Hard mud nests on walls and ceilings (mud daubers and potter wasps)
healthRisks: Stings are painful and cause swelling, and wasps can sting many times
Some people have severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) that can be life-threatening
Many stings at once can cause serious illness, including kidney damage, even without an allergy
Stings in the mouth or throat can cause dangerous swelling
safeSteps: Stay well back from nests and keep children and pets away; do not swat at wasps or throw things at a nest, and get medical care for any strong reaction to a sting
Get emergency medical care for trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips or throat, dizziness, fainting, a sting in the mouth or throat, or many stings
If many wasps or bees attack, run to a building or vehicle while covering your face; do not jump into water
Cover food and drinks outdoors, and check open drink cans before sipping
Keep garbage bins closed and pick up fallen fruit
Note where wasps fly to and from, and avoid that area
callProfessionalWhen: A nest is near doors, windows, play areas or walkways
A nest is inside a wall, roof or underground
Anyone in the home is allergic to stings
firstAid: Move away from the area
If a stinger is left in the skin (honey bee), scrape it out with a fingernail or card; do not squeeze it or use tweezers
Wash the sting with soap and water; a cold pack can ease swelling
Get emergency medical care for any sign of a severe allergic reaction or for many stings
If the person has a known sting allergy and a prescribed adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector, use it and go to hospital at once
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: Common indoor spiders, including cellar spiders with very long thin legs and small cobweb-building house spiders. They catch insects in their webs and are not considered medically important.
signs: Small-bodied spider with very long, thin legs hanging upside down in a loose web, shaking rapidly when disturbed (cellar spider)
Small yellowish-brown spider with a rounded, mottled abdomen in a tangled cobweb (common house spider)
Cobwebs in ceiling corners, windows, basements and behind furniture
Small, round, papery brown egg sacs in webs
healthRisks: Bites are rare and usually cause only short-lived local pain and redness
Not known to spread disease
safeSteps: Vacuum or sweep webs, spiders and egg sacs regularly
Move single spiders outdoors using a jar and a sheet of paper
Seal cracks and gaps around windows, doors and pipes, and keep screens in good repair
Reduce clutter, and store boxes off the floor and away from walls
Turn off outdoor lights near doors and windows or move them away, since lights attract the insects spiders eat
callProfessionalWhen: Spiders remain very numerous after cleaning, which may point to a large insect problem
firstAid: Wash a bite with soap and water
Get medical care for any unusual, spreading or severe reaction

cards.summary: Large, flat, fast-running brown spiders with long legs that spread sideways like a crab's. They hunt insects such as cockroaches on walls at night instead of catching them in webs; bites are uncommon but can be painful.
signs: Large brown spider with a leg span that can reach about 10 to 12 cm, legs spread sideways like a crab's
Flattened body; often seen high on walls or behind curtains, pictures and furniture at night
Very fast, sideways movement when disturbed
Females carrying a large, flat, white egg sac under the body
healthRisks: May bite if handled or trapped against the skin; bites can be painful with local swelling
Not known to spread disease
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not handle it. If it is a thick, hairy spider with bold black, white, grey or yellow patterns, it may be a protected ornamental tarantula: do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it. Otherwise, gently guide it into a large container and release it outdoors
Shake out clothes, towels and shoes that have been left on the floor
Seal gaps around doors, windows and vents
Reduce the cockroaches and other insects it feeds on
callProfessionalWhen: Many large spiders keep appearing indoors
The spider could be an ornamental tarantula; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash a bite with soap and water; a cold pack may ease local pain
Get medical care for severe pain, spreading swelling or any allergic reaction
cards.legal: Indian ornamental tarantulas (Poecilotheria) are listed in Schedule II of the schedules substituted by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022); common huntsman spiders are not listed. If a large, hairy, boldly patterned spider could be an ornamental tarantula, do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: Small, compact, often hairy spiders with large front eyes that stalk and jump on insects. They are common on walls, windows and plants and rarely bite.
signs: Small (usually under about 1.5 cm), stocky spider with two very large forward-facing eyes
Jerky walking and sudden jumps; turns to watch movement
Often seen in daylight on sunny walls, window sills and plants
Small silk retreats in the corners of window frames
healthRisks: Bites are uncommon and usually cause mild, short-lived pain
Not known to spread disease
safeSteps: Leave it alone outdoors, where it eats pest insects
If found indoors, move it outside with a jar and a sheet of paper
Seal gaps around windows and doors
callProfessionalWhen: Rarely needed; only if many spiders appear together with a large insect problem
firstAid: Wash a bite with soap and water, and get medical care for any unusual reaction

cards.summary: Spiders of the genus Latrodectus, including black and brown widows, with a shiny round abdomen often marked underneath with a red or orange hourglass. A bite from an adult female can cause serious illness and needs medical care.
signs: Shiny black or mottled brown spider with a round abdomen and a red, orange or yellow hourglass mark underneath (the mark may be faint or missing)
Messy, irregular, strong cobwebs in sheltered spots such as woodpiles, under furniture, in garages, sheds and outdoor toilets
Round egg sacs in the web: smooth and pale (black widow) or covered in small spikes like a pollen grain (brown widow)
Spider hanging upside down in the web, often at night
healthRisks: Bites from adult females can cause severe pain, muscle cramps, rigid stomach muscles, sweating, nausea, a fast heartbeat, high blood pressure and restlessness
Children, older adults and people in poor health are at higher risk
Bites are rare and usually happen when the spider is pressed against the skin
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not touch the spider or its web; if bitten, stay calm and get medical care promptly
Wear gloves when moving wood, stones, boxes or garden debris
Shake out shoes, gloves and clothes that have been stored or left outside
Reduce clutter and woodpiles near the house, and seal gaps around doors and windows
Store items in sealed bags or taped boxes kept off the floor
callProfessionalWhen: Widow spiders are found indoors or where children play
Several webs are found around the home
firstAid: Get medical care promptly for any suspected widow spider bite
Wash the bite with soap and water; a cold pack may ease the pain, and raise the bitten limb if possible
Do not cut, suck or squeeze the bite
If it can be done without going near the spider, photograph it to show the doctor
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: Brown spiders of the genus Loxosceles that hide in dry, undisturbed places. A bite can sometimes cause a slow-healing skin wound; most brown spiders people find turn out to be other species.
signs: Light to medium brown spider of one even colour, body up to about 1 cm, with long thin legs
Six eyes in three pairs (most spiders have eight); a dark violin-shaped mark behind the eyes may be present but is not a reliable sign
Legs without spines and of one colour; abdomen of one colour with fine hairs
Found in dark, undisturbed places such as boxes, cupboards, behind furniture, in shoes and in storerooms
healthRisks: Most bites cause only redness and swelling, but some cause a spreading sore or skin damage that needs medical care
Rarely, especially in children, a bite can cause fever, chills, vomiting, dark urine or body-wide illness, which needs urgent hospital care
Many skin wounds blamed on spider bites have other causes, such as bacterial infections, so a doctor's assessment matters
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not handle the spider; if bitten, get medical care
Shake out clothes, shoes and bedding that have been stored or left on the floor
Move beds away from walls and clear items stored under beds
Store seldom-used items in sealed boxes and reduce clutter

Seal cracks and utility openings; to see where spiders are active, place small covered monitoring traps inside cupboards and storerooms, out of reach of children, pets and lizards, and check them daily
callProfessionalWhen: Several spiders that look like recluse spiders are found in the home
You are not sure of the identification; an expert can check a clear photo taken from well back
firstAid: Get medical care for any suspected recluse bite, especially if a blister, spreading redness or a dark sore develops
Wash the bite with soap and water and apply a cold pack
Do not cut, suck or squeeze the bite
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: Robust, hairy, brown or grey ground-hunting spiders that chase their prey instead of using webs. Females carry their egg sac and spiderlings on their bodies; bites are uncommon and usually mild but can be painful.
signs: Robust brown or grey spider, often with darker stripes on the back, running across floors and the ground
Female carrying a round egg sac attached to the rear of the body, or many spiderlings on her back
Eyes that shine back when lit by a torch at night
Found under stones, boards, firewood and along walls, mainly at night
healthRisks: May bite if handled or trapped against the skin, causing pain, redness and swelling that usually fade within a day
Not known to spread disease
safeSteps: Stay well back and avoid handling it; move it outdoors with a jar and a sheet of paper
Seal gaps under doors and around windows and pipes
Clear firewood, stones, boards and debris from near the walls
Reduce outdoor lighting near doors, which attracts the insects it hunts
callProfessionalWhen: Many spiders keep entering the house
firstAid: Wash a bite with soap and water
Get medical care for severe pain, spreading redness or any allergic reaction

cards.summary: Eight-legged animals with pincers and a curved tail that ends in a stinger, active at night. In India, the Indian red scorpion (Hottentotta tamulus) is medically important: its sting can cause life-threatening illness, especially in children.
signs: Animal with a pair of pincers and a segmented tail curved over the back, ending in a stinger
Reddish-brown to orange, about 5 to 9 cm (Indian red scorpion), or larger and black (forest scorpions)
Hiding by day under stones, bricks, firewood, debris, shoes or cloth and in wall cracks; active at night
Glows blue-green under ultraviolet (UV) light
healthRisks: Stings cause intense burning pain, and a sting from the Indian red scorpion can lead to severe illness affecting the heart and lungs

Warning signs that need urgent hospital care: vomiting, heavy sweating, drooling, cold hands and feet, a very fast or very slow heartbeat, restlessness, chest discomfort, breathing difficulty, or a persistent painful erection in boys and men
Children and older adults are at the highest risk
Do not judge the danger by the scorpion's size or colour; every sting in a child is an emergency
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not try to pick up or corner a scorpion; any sting in a child, or any sting followed by sweating, vomiting or breathing trouble, needs urgent hospital care
Shake out shoes, clothes, towels and bedding before use, and use a torch when walking at night
Wear shoes outdoors, and gloves when moving bricks, stones, firewood or debris
Clear debris, stones and firewood away from the house, and check firewood before bringing it inside
Seal cracks in walls and floors, fit door sweeps, and keep window screens in repair
Keep beds and cots away from walls, and keep bedding from touching the floor
callProfessionalWhen: Scorpions are found indoors more than once
You live near fields, rocks or construction debris where many scorpions are seen
firstAid: Go to the nearest hospital or health centre quickly, especially for children; do not wait for symptoms to get worse
Keep the person calm and still
Do not cut or suck the sting site, and do not tie a tight band
Do not put herbs, pastes or anything else on the sting, and do not go to traditional healers instead of hospital, which can delay care
Note the time of the sting and, if it can be done without going near it, photograph the scorpion for the doctor
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: Large, flat, segmented centipedes, often 10 cm or longer, with one pair of legs per segment and a pair of strong biting claws behind the head. They hunt at night and can give a very painful bite.
signs: Long, flattened body with many segments and one pair of legs on each segment; often reddish, orange, brown or blue-black
Fast, snake-like running; does not curl into a coil like a millipede
Hiding under stones, bricks, logs, leaf litter and damp cloth, and in bathrooms or drains
Active at night, especially in the rainy season
healthRisks: Bites cause intense pain, swelling, redness and sometimes numbness
Rarely, bites cause a severe allergic reaction, heart strain with chest pain, or a serious wound infection; children are at higher risk
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not try to pick it up, even with gloves; if bitten, get medical care
Shake out shoes, clothes and bedding, especially in the rainy season
Wear gloves and shoes when moving stones, bricks, wood or garden debris
Clear leaf litter, rotting wood and debris away from the house, and keep bathrooms and storage areas dry
Seal cracks and gaps under doors, and screen drains
callProfessionalWhen: Large centipedes are found indoors repeatedly
firstAid: Wash the bite with soap and water
Get medical care for severe pain or spreading swelling, especially in children
Get emergency care for chest pain, trouble breathing, swelling of the face or fainting
See a doctor if redness spreads, pus forms or fever starts in the days after the bite
Do not cut the bite, and do not put herbs, pastes or anything else on it
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: A small grey-brown rodent with large ears and a long tail that lives in and around buildings, eating and fouling stored food. Its droppings, urine and nests can spread illness.
signs: Small rodent, body about 7 to 9 cm, with large ears, a pointed snout and a thin tail about as long as the body
Small rod-shaped droppings about 3 to 6 mm long, often pointed at the ends, near food, in drawers and in cupboards
Gnawed packets, holes in food bags and small gnaw marks on wood or wires
Nests of finely shredded paper, cloth or other soft material behind boxes or appliances
Scratching, scurrying and squeaking at night, and a musky smell where many live
healthRisks: Urine, droppings and saliva can carry germs that cause illnesses such as salmonella infection, leptospirosis and lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM)
LCM infection in pregnancy can cause miscarriage or serious birth defects; pregnant women should avoid mice and their droppings
Bites, scratches or contact with mouse saliva or urine can pass on rat-bite fever
Mouse allergens can trigger asthma, especially in children
Gnawed electrical wires can cause fires
safeSteps: Stay well back from mice, droppings and nests, do not touch them with bare hands, keep children and pets away, and get medical care for any bite

Before cleaning up droppings, urine or nests, open doors and windows for 30 minutes; then, wearing gloves, soak them with a household disinfectant for 5 minutes, wipe them up with paper towels and throw them away in a closed bag; do not sweep or vacuum them dry, and wash hands with soap and water afterwards
Seal gaps larger than about 6 mm with metal mesh, sheet metal or cement; plastic, rubber, foam and wood are easily gnawed
Store food and grain in metal, glass or thick plastic containers with tight lids, and clean up spills
Reduce clutter and nesting places, and keep garbage in closed bins
Avoid wading, bathing or swimming in floodwater or muddy water that may hold rat urine; wear boots and cover cuts with waterproof dressings
Do not use glue boards (sticky rat traps); rodents, shrews, lizards and birds caught on them suffer for a long time, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban them
Where lawful, set snap traps along walls and in dark corners, out of reach of children and pets, check them daily, and handle traps and dead mice with gloves
callProfessionalWhen: Droppings keep appearing after a few weeks of sealing and trapping
Mice are in food stores, shops, kitchens or many rooms
firstAid: Wash any bite or scratch with soap and running water and get medical care
See a doctor for fever, body aches or yellow eyes after contact with rodents or their urine, and mention the contact; rat-bite fever can start up to three weeks after contact
Watch for fever for up to 30 days after contact with floodwater; passing little urine, breathlessness or coughing blood is an emergency, so go to hospital at once
Ask the doctor whether you need a tetanus injection
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
cards.legal: Common house rats, house mice and bandicoot rats are not listed in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022; the old vermin schedule that named rats and mice was removed, and only a few rare forest rats and mice are listed (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, still applies to how any animal is trapped, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban glue traps.

cards.summary: A slender, agile rat with a pointed snout, large ears and a tail longer than its body that climbs well and often lives in roofs, ceilings, stores and trees. It is a common house rat in much of India.
signs: Slender dark grey-brown to black rat; tail longer than the head and body, and ears large enough to reach the eyes when folded forward
Spindle-shaped droppings about 1 to 1.5 cm long, pointed at the ends
Running, scratching or gnawing noises in ceilings, roofs and walls at night
Dark greasy rub marks along beams, pipes and walls
Gnawed fruit, grain sacks, wires and packaging, especially in high places
healthRisks: Urine and droppings can spread leptospirosis, especially during floods and heavy rain
Rats can spread rat-bite fever, salmonella and murine typhus, and their fleas have spread plague
Gnawed wiring can cause fires
safeSteps: Stay well back from rats, droppings and nests, do not touch them with bare hands, keep children and pets away, and get medical care for any rat bite or scratch

Before cleaning up droppings, urine or nests, open doors and windows for 30 minutes; then, wearing gloves, soak them with a household disinfectant for 5 minutes, wipe them up with paper towels and throw them away in a closed bag; do not sweep or vacuum them dry, and wash hands with soap and water afterwards
Trim tree branches and creepers away from the roof, and seal roof and wall gaps larger than about 6 mm with metal mesh or sheet metal
Cover vents and drains with strong metal mesh
Store food, grain and animal feed in metal or other containers rats cannot easily gnaw through, and keep garbage in closed bins
Avoid wading, bathing or swimming in floodwater or muddy water that may hold rat urine; wear boots and cover cuts with waterproof dressings
Do not use glue boards (sticky rat traps); rodents, shrews, lizards and birds caught on them suffer for a long time, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban them

Where lawful, set snap traps only inside closed rooms or covered boxes that squirrels, birds and civets cannot enter; set them after dark, close them at dawn, and check them daily. If any animal other than a rat is caught or hurt, contact the State Forest Department
callProfessionalWhen: Rats are seen in daylight, or there are many droppings in several places
Rats are in grain stores, shops or food businesses
Several dead rats are found; also inform your local health department

Heavy thumping in the roof at night, a strong musky smell, or a pile of seed-filled droppings in one spot may mean an Asian palm civet, which is protected; do not trap it, and contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash bites and scratches with soap and running water and get medical care
See a doctor promptly for fever, muscle pain, red eyes or yellow eyes after contact with rats or floodwater; rat-bite fever can start up to three weeks after a bite or scratch
Watch for fever for up to 30 days after contact with floodwater; passing little urine, breathlessness or coughing blood is an emergency, so go to hospital at once
Ask the doctor whether you need a tetanus injection
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
cards.legal: Common house rats, house mice and bandicoot rats are not listed in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022; the old vermin schedule that named rats and mice was removed, and only a few rare forest rats and mice are listed (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, still applies to how any animal is trapped, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban glue traps.

cards.summary: A large, heavy-bodied rat with a blunt snout, small ears and a tail shorter than its body that burrows in soil and lives in sewers, drains and ground floors. It is common in cities and ports.
signs: Large grey-brown rat with a blunt muzzle, small ears and a thick tail shorter than the head and body, dark above and pale below
Capsule-shaped droppings with blunt ends, about 1.5 to 2 cm long
Burrows along foundations and under garbage bins, woodpiles and drains
Greasy rub marks low along walls, and gnawing or scratching sounds at floor level at night
healthRisks: Urine and droppings can spread leptospirosis, especially during floods and heavy rain
Rats can spread rat-bite fever, salmonella and murine typhus
Their fleas can carry plague; do not handle dead rats, and report several dead rats to the health department
Gnawed wiring and pipes can cause fires and leaks
safeSteps: Stay well back from rats, droppings and nests, do not touch them with bare hands, keep children and pets away, and get medical care for any rat bite or scratch

Before cleaning up droppings, urine or nests, open doors and windows for 30 minutes; then, wearing gloves, soak them with a household disinfectant for 5 minutes, wipe them up with paper towels and throw them away in a closed bag; do not sweep or vacuum them dry, and wash hands with soap and water afterwards
Seal gaps at ground level and around pipes larger than about 6 mm with metal mesh, sheet metal or cement
Cover drains and floor traps with strong grates, and repair broken drain and sewer pipes
Remove garbage, debris and woodpiles near the building, and keep bins closed
Avoid wading, bathing or swimming in floodwater or muddy water that may hold rat urine; wear boots and cover cuts with waterproof dressings
Do not use glue boards (sticky rat traps); rodents, shrews, lizards and birds caught on them suffer for a long time, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban them
Where lawful, set snap traps flush against walls in dark corners, inside covered boxes that children, pets and birds cannot reach, and check them daily
callProfessionalWhen: Rats are seen in daylight, or burrows are found around the building
Rats are coming from sewers or drains; also inform your municipal office
Rats are in food stores, shops or food businesses
firstAid: Wash bites and scratches with soap and running water and get medical care
See a doctor promptly for fever, muscle pain, red eyes or yellow eyes after contact with rats or floodwater; rat-bite fever can start up to three weeks after a bite or scratch
Watch for fever for up to 30 days after contact with floodwater; passing little urine, breathlessness or coughing blood is an emergency, so go to hospital at once
Ask the doctor whether you need a tetanus injection
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
cards.legal: Common house rats, house mice and bandicoot rats are not listed in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022; the old vermin schedule that named rats and mice was removed, and only a few rare forest rats and mice are listed (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, still applies to how any animal is trapped, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban glue traps.

cards.summary: Large, heavy rats of South Asia (Bandicota) that dig extensive burrows in fields, gardens, godowns and under buildings. They damage and hoard stored grain and are an important rodent pest in India.
signs: Large, dark grey-brown rat with a rounded head, long coarse hair and a tail shorter than the body; may raise its hair and grunt when cornered
Burrow openings with fresh mounds of loose soil in fields and gardens, along walls and under floors
Large droppings, and grain or soil spilling from holes in the floors and walls of stores
Grain hoarded inside burrows, and damage to sacks, floors and drains
healthRisks: Can spread leptospirosis and other rat-borne infections through urine and droppings
Their fleas can carry plague; several dead rats in one place should be reported to health authorities
May bite when cornered
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not corner or handle bandicoot rats; get medical care for any bite
Store grain in metal bins or on raised platforms, and keep storerooms clear of spilled grain
Build or repair floors and walls with concrete, and fit metal sheets or mesh at the base of doors
Close or firm down burrow openings and check the next day; reopened burrows show where rats are active. Never put hands into burrows; snakes often shelter in rat burrows
Clear weeds, debris and garbage near stores and houses
Avoid wading, bathing or swimming in floodwater or muddy water that may hold rat urine; wear boots and cover cuts with waterproof dressings
Do not use glue boards (sticky rat traps); rodents, shrews, lizards and birds caught on them suffer for a long time, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban them

Where lawful, set strong snap traps inside covered runways or boxes that mongooses, squirrels, birds and snakes cannot enter, and check them daily. If a mongoose, snake or other wild animal is caught or hurt, contact the State Forest Department
callProfessionalWhen: There are many active burrows in godowns, warehouses or around buildings; call a licensed pest-control professional
For rats in fields, contact your local agricultural extension office or Krishi Vigyan Kendra
firstAid: Wash bites and scratches with soap and running water and get medical care
See a doctor promptly for fever, muscle pain, red eyes or yellow eyes after contact with rats, their burrows or floodwater
Watch for fever for up to 30 days after contact with floodwater; passing little urine, breathlessness or coughing blood is an emergency, so go to hospital at once
Ask the doctor whether you need a tetanus injection
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
cards.legal: Common house rats, house mice and bandicoot rats are not listed in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022; the old vermin schedule that named rats and mice was removed, and only a few rare forest rats and mice are listed (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, still applies to how any animal is trapped, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban glue traps.

cards.summary: A grey, mouse-sized, insect-eating mammal (Suncus murinus) with a long pointed snout and a strong musky smell, often mistaken for a mouse or rat. It is not a rodent, but it can carry leptospirosis, and its droppings and smell can foul stored food.
signs: Grey to brownish-grey velvety fur, a long, pointed, twitching snout, tiny eyes and small ears
Runs along walls at night, often making high-pitched chattering, clicking or chirping sounds
A strong musky smell in rooms or on food it has touched
Five clawed toes on each foot
healthRisks: Can bite if handled
Can carry leptospirosis germs in its urine, like rats
Droppings and its musky smell can contaminate stored food, and it may carry fleas
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not handle it with bare hands, as it may bite; open a door and gently guide it outside with a broom, and get medical care for any bite
Seal gaps under doors and around pipes and drains
Store food in closed containers and keep floors free of food scraps
Reduce the cockroaches and other insects it feeds on

Before cleaning up droppings, urine or nests, open doors and windows for 30 minutes; then, wearing gloves, soak them with a household disinfectant for 5 minutes, wipe them up with paper towels and throw them away in a closed bag; do not sweep or vacuum them dry, and wash hands with soap and water afterwards
Do not use glue boards (sticky rat traps); rodents, shrews, lizards and birds caught on them suffer for a long time, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban them
callProfessionalWhen: Shrews or their droppings keep appearing in food stores or kitchens
firstAid: Wash any bite with soap and running water and get medical care
See a doctor for fever, muscle pain, or red or yellow eyes after contact with shrews or their droppings
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
cards.legal: The Asian house shrew (Suncus murinus) is not listed in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022; a rare relative, Day's shrew (Suncus dayi), is listed in Schedule I (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, still applies to how any animal is trapped.

cards.summary: Small grey-brown squirrels with three or five pale stripes along the back and a bushy tail, common around homes and gardens in India; they are active by day and sometimes nest in roofs, ducts and cupboards. The five-striped palm squirrel is protected under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
signs: Small squirrel with three (mainly southern India) or five (mainly northern India) pale stripes on a grey-brown back, and a bushy tail
Active in daylight, running along walls, trees, wires and roofs
Loud, repeated, high-pitched chirping calls, often with tail flicks
Nests of grass, cloth and fibre in roof spaces, air-conditioner ducts, false ceilings or cupboards
Gnawed fruit, seeds and grain left out to dry, and sometimes gnawed wires
healthRisks: May bite or scratch if handled or cornered
Bites or scratches can rarely pass on rat-bite fever
Can carry fleas and mites
safeSteps: Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
Stay well back and do not try to handle squirrels; let them leave on their own, and get medical care for any bite or scratch
Do not feed squirrels near the house, and cover grain and food set out to dry
Before sealing a hole, check that no squirrels or babies are inside: plug it loosely with paper and see whether it is pushed out
Seal gaps under eaves, at roof joints and around ducts with metal mesh only after the squirrels have left; never seal in young or remove a nest yourself
Trim branches that touch the roof or the wires leading to the house

Do not use glue boards (sticky traps) or rat traps where squirrels go; squirrels, rats, lizards and birds caught on glue boards suffer for a long time, and the Animal Welfare Board of India has directed states to ban them
callProfessionalWhen: A squirrel is trapped indoors or injured, or babies are in a nest that has to be moved; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash any bite or scratch with soap and running water and get medical care
See a doctor for fever in the three weeks after a bite or scratch
Ask the doctor whether you need a tetanus injection
cards.legal: The five-striped palm squirrel (Funambulus pennantii) is a protected wild animal: it is listed in Schedule II of the schedules substituted by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (Schedule IV under the 1972 Act) (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Under the Act, hunting includes capturing, trapping or injuring an animal, and hunting a Schedule II animal is an offence. The three-striped palm squirrel (Funambulus palmarum) is hard to tell apart from it, so regard every palm squirrel as protected and do not disturb its nests. Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: Small, pale grey to brown lizards (Hemidactylus) with sticky toe pads that climb walls and ceilings and hunt insects near lights at night. They are common in Indian homes; they rarely bite, and the bite is weak.
signs: Small lizard, about 7 to 15 cm long, pale grey, pinkish or brown and sometimes see-through, clinging to walls and ceilings
Gathers near lights at night to catch insects
Repeated chirping or clicking 'tchuk-tchuk' calls, by day or night
Small dark droppings with a white tip on floors, window sills and shelves
A dropped tail that keeps wriggling for a while
healthRisks: Reptiles, including geckos, can carry Salmonella germs, and droppings can contaminate food and surfaces
May give a weak bite if handled
safeSteps: Leave it alone where possible; it eats insects such as mosquitoes and cockroaches
Keep food and water covered, wipe up droppings with a paper towel or gloves, and then wash hands with soap and water
If you are sure it is a common house gecko, place a box over it, slide a card underneath and release it outdoors
Seal gaps of about 6 mm or more around doors, windows, pipes and vents, and use door sweeps and window screens
Use yellow or fewer outdoor lights to attract fewer of the insects that geckos follow
callProfessionalWhen: Rarely needed; if a large, blue-grey gecko with orange or red spots is found (possibly a protected Tokay gecko), do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash hands, and any bite, with soap and water
Throw away food a lizard has fallen into or fouled; germs can cause vomiting or diarrhoea, so see a doctor if these start
cards.legal: Common house geckos (Hemidactylus) are not named in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022. Some geckos are: the Tokay gecko (Gekko gecko) is listed in Schedule I, and several other geckos, including leopard geckos (Eublepharis), in Schedule II (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). If you are not sure of the species, do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: A slender, long-tailed lizard (Calotes versicolor) with a crest of spines along the back, common on walls, fences and garden plants in India. Breeding males can turn bright orange to red on the head and throat.
signs: Light brown to olive lizard with a long thin tail and a row of spines along the neck and back
Males with a bright orange or red head and throat in the breeding season
Active by day, basking on walls, fences, hedges and tree trunks, and bobbing its head
Changes colour from brown to darker or brighter shades
Often called गिरगिट in Hindi, a name also used for the protected Indian chameleon; check for turret-like eyes and gripping feet
healthRisks: Reptiles can carry Salmonella germs
May bite if caught or handled
safeSteps: Leave it alone outdoors, where it eats insects
Do not handle it; if one comes indoors, open a door or window and give it a clear way out
Wash hands with soap and water after touching anything it has been on
Seal gaps around doors and windows to keep lizards out
callProfessionalWhen: Rarely needed; if the animal could be a chameleon (slow-moving, with turret-like eyes and gripping feet), do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash any bite with soap and water
cards.legal: The oriental garden lizard (Calotes versicolor) is not named in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022. The look-alike Indian chameleon (Chamaeleo zeylanicus) is listed in Schedule I (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). If it could be a chameleon, do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: Smooth, shiny lizards with short legs and a long body that move quickly through leaf litter and gardens and sometimes into ground-floor rooms. Common Indian skinks (Eutropis) are brown or bronze, often with stripes, and can be mistaken for small snakes.
signs: Shiny, smooth, tightly overlapping scales that look polished or wet
Short legs and a long body; moves with a snake-like wriggle
Brown or bronze with darker or pale stripes along the sides
Active by day on the ground, in leaf litter, gardens, stone walls and ground-floor rooms
healthRisks: Reptiles can carry Salmonella germs
May bite if caught or handled; the bite is minor
safeSteps: If you are not sure whether it is a skink or a small snake, stay well back and keep children and pets away
Leave it alone outdoors, where it eats insects
If one comes indoors, open a door and give it a clear way out, or guide it into a box and release it outside
Wash hands with soap and water after touching anything it has been on
Seal gaps under doors and around pipes
callProfessionalWhen: Rarely needed; if you are not sure whether it is a skink or a snake, stay well back and contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash any bite with soap and water
If you think it may have been a snake bite, keep the person still and go to hospital at once
cards.legal: Common skinks (Eutropis) are not named in Schedule I or II of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022 (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Skinks can be mistaken for small snakes, and many Indian snakes are listed. If you are not sure, do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: Large lizards (Varanus) with a long neck, a forked tongue, strong claws and a long, powerful tail; the Bengal monitor can reach about 1.75 m including the tail. Indian monitor lizards are protected under Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
signs: Large grey, brown or olive lizard, often 60 cm to over 1.5 m long including the tail, with a long neck and loose skin
Long forked tongue flicking in and out like a snake's
Strong legs with curved claws; walks with the body raised and the tail swinging
Deep claw marks and a tail-drag line in soft soil
Loud hissing and body puffing when cornered
healthRisks: Can bite, scratch with strong claws and lash with its tail if cornered or handled, causing deep wounds
Reptiles can carry Salmonella germs, and wounds can become infected
safeSteps: Stay well back and keep children and pets away; do not corner it, and leave it a clear way out
Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
If it is inside a room, close inner doors, open a door to the outside and leave the room quietly
Note where it went and wait for help to arrive instead of trying to catch it yourself
callProfessionalWhen: It is inside a home, shop or store, or it is injured or trapped; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash any bite or scratch with soap and running water and get medical care, as wounds can become infected
Ask the doctor whether you need a tetanus injection
cards.legal: Bengal, desert, water and yellow monitor lizards (Varanus bengalensis, Varanus griseus, Varanus salvator and Varanus flavescens) are listed in Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as substituted by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Hunting them, which under the Act includes capturing, trapping, injuring or disturbing their eggs or nests, is an offence, as is trading in them or their parts. Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: Many kinds of snakes live around Indian homes, fields and stores, often hunting rats; a few, especially cobras, kraits, Russell's vipers and saw-scaled vipers, have bites that can cause death or lasting disability. Many Indian snakes are also protected by law.
signs: Long, legless body covered in scales, with no eyelids and no ear openings
Tongue flicking in and out; moves in S-shaped curves
Shed skins in roofs, stores, wood piles or around rat burrows
Seen at dusk or at night near rat burrows, grain stores, cattle sheds, wood piles and drains, especially in the rainy season
A raised hood (cobras) or a loud hiss or rasping sound (vipers) when disturbed
Glossy black or blue-black body with thin white cross-bands (common krait), often found indoors at night
healthRisks: Bites from cobras, kraits, Russell's vipers and saw-scaled vipers can cause death or lasting disability
Krait bites often happen at night to people sleeping on the floor and may be almost painless; stomach pain, weakness or drooping eyelids can be the first signs
Even a dead snake, or its cut-off head, can still bite
safeSteps: Stay well back from any snake, even one that looks dead, and keep children and pets away; if anyone is bitten, go to hospital at once
Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
If a snake is inside, leave the room, keep others out, and watch where it goes from well back until help arrives
Sleep on a raised bed under a tucked-in mosquito net, especially in the rainy season
Use a torch and wear shoes when walking outside at night
Keep rats away, since snakes follow them: store grain in closed bins, and clear rubbish, wood piles and tall grass from around the house
Do not put hands into holes, burrows, wood piles or dark corners you cannot see into, and check shoes and bedding before use
callProfessionalWhen: Any snake is inside a home, store or cattle shed, or keeps coming back; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
A snake is injured or trapped, for example in netting; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Move away from the snake; do not try to catch it or touch it, even if it looks dead
Keep the person calm and still, keep the bitten limb still, and remove rings, watches and tight clothing
Go at once to the nearest hospital that can give anti-snake serum (ASV); do not wait for symptoms, and do not let the person drive
Do not cut or suck the bite, tie a tight band, apply ice or electric shock, or use herbs or traditional healers
Do not give alcohol, aspirin or ibuprofen
Stomach pain, weakness or drooping eyelids after a night sleeping on the floor may be a krait bite even without a visible mark; go to hospital at once
If it can be done from well back, photograph the snake for the doctor, but do not delay going to hospital
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
cards.legal: Many Indian snakes are listed in the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2022, including the Indian rock python and king cobra (Schedule I) and the spectacled cobra and rat snake (Schedule II) (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Hunting a listed snake, which under the Act includes capturing, trapping or injuring it, is an offence. Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
