cards.summary: A slow-moving lizard (Chamaeleo zeylanicus) with a tall, flattened body, eyes that turn separately, gripping feet and a curling tail, found in trees and hedges in much of India. It is protected under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
signs: Green, yellow or brown lizard with a tall, flattened body and a raised, helmet-like head
Large cone-shaped (turret) eyes that move separately in different directions
Toes joined into two gripping bundles on each foot, like tongs, and a tail that curls around twigs
Very slow, swaying walk along branches; changes colour, often darkening when disturbed
Catches insects with a very long tongue
healthRisks: May hiss or bite if handled
Reptiles can carry Salmonella germs
safeSteps: Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
Stay well back, keep children and pets away, and let it move on by itself
If it is indoors or on a road, keep people and pets away and wait for help instead of picking it up
Wash hands with soap and water after touching anything it has been on
callProfessionalWhen: It is injured, trapped or inside a building, or someone is catching or keeping one; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash hands, and any bite or scratch, with soap and water
cards.legal: The Indian chameleon (Chamaeleo zeylanicus) is listed in Schedule I of the schedules substituted by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Hunting it, which under the Act includes capturing, trapping or injuring it, and trading in it or its parts are offences. Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: A large, heavy-bodied gecko (Gekko gecko), up to about 35 cm long, grey or blue-grey with orange to red spots, found in north-east India and nearby regions. It is protected under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
signs: Large gecko, much bigger than a house gecko, with a big head, velvety skin and grey or blue-grey colour with orange, red or rust spots
Loud, repeated 'to-kay' call, mainly at night
Wide toe pads; clings to walls, tree trunks and roofs, mostly at night
Opens its mouth wide, hisses or croaks when approached
healthRisks: Can give a strong, painful bite and may hold on if handled
Reptiles can carry Salmonella germs
safeSteps: Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
Stay well back and do not try to pick it up; it bites hard
If it is indoors, keep children and pets out of the room and leave a door or window open so it can leave
Wash hands with soap and water after touching anything it has been on
callProfessionalWhen: It is inside a home, injured or trapped, or someone is catching or keeping one; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: Wash any bite with soap and running water; see a doctor if it is deep or becomes red, swollen or painful
cards.legal: The Tokay gecko (Gekko gecko) is listed in Schedule I of the schedules substituted by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Hunting it, which under the Act includes capturing, trapping or injuring it, and trading in it or its parts are offences. Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: A cat-sized, long-tailed mammal (Paradoxurus hermaphroditus) with a pale face mask and a grey to black coat that is active at night, eats mostly fruit and often rests in roofs, attics and trees near homes. It is protected under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
signs: Cat-sized animal, body about 50 cm with a tail nearly as long, grey to black fur with dark stripes or rows of spots, and pale patches around the eyes and nose
Heavy thumping, walking and scratching in the roof or attic at night
Droppings full of fruit seeds, often piled in one spot on roofs, walls or ledges
A strong musky smell
Eaten fruit such as papaya, mango, banana and chiku, and visits to palm-sap pots
healthRisks: May bite and scratch hard if cornered, trapped or handled
Like other mammals, it can carry rabies; any bite or scratch needs a doctor's advice the same day
safeSteps: Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
Stay well back, keep children and pets away, and do not corner it
Do not set rat traps where a civet can reach them, and do not use glue boards
Pick up fallen fruit, and cover food and grain at night
Close roof gaps only after the civet has gone out at night, and never seal in young; ask the Forest Department for help if young may be inside
callProfessionalWhen: A civet is living in the roof or attic, is injured or trapped, or has young indoors; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: If bitten or scratched, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and see a doctor the same day about rabies
Ask the doctor whether you need a tetanus injection
cards.legal: The Asian palm civet (Paradoxurus hermaphroditus) is listed in Schedule I of the schedules substituted by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (Schedule II under the 1972 Act) (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Hunting it, which under the Act includes capturing, trapping or injuring it, and trading in it or its parts are offences. Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

names.en: Bat (Indian flying fox and other bats)

cards.summary: Flying mammals that are active at night; the Indian flying fox (Pteropus giganteus) is a large fruit bat with a wingspan of about 1.2 to 1.5 m that roosts in big colonies in tall trees, while smaller insect-eating bats roost in roofs, walls and caves. The Indian flying fox and several other bats are protected under the Wild Life (Protection) Act.
signs: Large bats with a fox-like face and dark wings hanging upside down in noisy colonies in tall trees such as banyan, fig or tamarind, often near water (flying fox)
Bats flying out at dusk and returning before dawn
Small dark droppings piling up under a roost in a roof, wall or ceiling gap
High-pitched squeaks and rustling from roof or wall gaps around dusk
Half-eaten fruit, chewed pulp and spat-out fibre under fruit trees (fruit bats)
healthRisks: Bats can carry rabies; any bite or scratch, even a small one, needs a doctor the same day
Fruit bats carry Nipah virus, which has caused outbreaks in India; people can be infected by eating fruit or drinking raw palm sap that bats have reached
safeSteps: Stay well back and do not touch any bat with bare hands, even one that is injured or looks dead; keep children and pets away
Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.
Throw away fruit with bite marks or that bats may have reached, and wash and peel fruit before eating
Do not drink raw, freshly collected palm sap; boil it first, and keep bats away from sap pots with covers
If bats roost in a roof or wall, do not block the gaps yourself while they are inside; ask the Forest Department for advice
callProfessionalWhen: A bat is inside a room, injured or on the ground, or a colony is roosting in a building; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it
firstAid: If bitten or scratched by any bat, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and go to a doctor or government hospital at once about rabies vaccination
Get medical care quickly for fever, headache, cough, breathing difficulty or confusion after contact with bats or with fruit or sap they may have reached, and mention it
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
cards.legal: The Indian flying fox (Pteropus giganteus) is listed in Schedule II, and several rare bats in Schedule I, of the schedules substituted by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022; under the 1972 Act fruit bats were classed as vermin (schedule to be confirmed by an expert against the Gazette of Act 18 of 2022). Bats are hard to tell apart, so regard every bat as protected. Do not harm, catch or injure it; contact the State Forest Department or a rescuer authorised by it.

cards.summary: A tiny, hairy fly, about 1.5 to 3.5 mm long or about a quarter the size of a mosquito, that breeds in warm, damp places rich in organic matter. In parts of Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, the sand fly Phlebotomus argentipes spreads kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis).
signs: Very small fly, much smaller than a mosquito, with the body and wings covered in long hairs and large wings held upright
Found in warm, humid places with damp soil and organic matter, in and around poorly built houses and animal sheds
Bites at night, often while people sleep on the floor or outdoors
healthRisks: Spreads kala-azar, which causes repeated fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, a swollen belly from an enlarged spleen and anaemia, and is usually fatal without medical care
Kala-azar can darken the skin, which gives it its name, 'black fever'
Months or years after kala-azar, some people get a rash on the face, arms or body (PKDL), which also needs a doctor
safeSteps: Get medical care and a kala-azar test at a government health centre for repeated fever, weight loss or a swollen belly, especially in Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh or West Bengal
Sleep on a raised bed under a bed net, not on the floor or outdoors
Repair cracks in walls and floors, and keep the house and animal sheds clean and dry, since poor housing gives sand flies places to rest and breed
Clear damp rubbish and organic waste from around the house
Follow your local health worker's advice during kala-azar campaigns
callProfessionalWhen: Several people in the village have long-lasting or repeated fever; inform your ASHA worker or the local health centre
firstAid: Get medical care for fever that keeps coming back, weight loss or a swollen belly, and mention that you live in or visited a kala-azar area
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency

cards.summary: The tiny larvae of trombiculid mites, barely visible to the eye, that live in grass, bushes and scrub and bite people who walk or work there. Infected chiggers spread scrub typhus, which occurs in rural parts of the Indian subcontinent.
signs: Tiny red or orange specks, smaller than a pinhead, on skin or clothes after time in grass or bushes
A dark, scab-like spot (eschar) at the bite site, often with fever
Bites after working or walking in fields, scrub, grass or bushes
healthRisks: Infected chiggers spread scrub typhus, which causes fever and chills, headache, body aches, swollen glands, a rash and sometimes confusion, usually within 10 days of the bite
Without early medical care, scrub typhus can damage organs, cause severe bleeding and can be fatal
There is no vaccine for scrub typhus
safeSteps: Get medical care quickly for fever after time in fields, scrub or bushes, and mention it; early care matters
Wear clothes that cover arms and legs, and shoes, when working in fields, grass or scrub, and dress children the same way
Where you can, avoid areas thick with vegetation and brush, and do not sit or lie directly on the grass
callProfessionalWhen: Several people in the area have fever after field work; inform your ASHA worker or the local health centre
firstAid: See a doctor at once for fever with a dark scab (eschar) on the skin
Go to hospital at once for confusion or extreme drowsiness
Call 112 or 108 for an ambulance in an emergency
